<margin>This is the verification of having already reached the limit of frugality.</margin>
<margin>Retreating is also regret.</margin>
<margin>Writing style note: circle</margin>
<margin>Not reaching</margin>
<margin>Writing style note: circle</margin>
<margin>Always like this</margin>
<margin>It is not that one acts because one considers it proper to act. "Fu" <gloss>to wear/bear</gloss> here is like the "fu" in "wearing on the chest" <note>referring to the phrase "holding fast to" or "bearing in mind"</note>.</margin>
<margin>And if one then contends with them, calamity will arrive.</margin>
<margin>Sentence structure note: circle</margin>
<margin>That which I practice</margin>
<margin>Appearance of walking sideways</margin>

Drinking, the old master <term>Laozi</term> <gloss>Old Master</gloss> remained indifferent and did not respond. The next day, Shicheng Qi saw him again and said,

### Commentary
In the past, I criticized you. Today, my heart is centered and has turned away from those thoughts. Why is this? Laozi said: As for those who are clever, wise, and saintly, I consider myself free from such things. In the past, if you called me an ox, I would acknowledge it as an ox. If you called me a horse, I would acknowledge it as a horse. If the reality exists, and someone gives it a name, if I do not accept it, I will suffer disaster again. My "wearing" <note>bearing or conduct</note> is constant. I do not "wear" <note>adhere to or act upon</note> because there is something to "wear." Shicheng Qi <unclear>holds fast to his conduct, avoids shadows, and treads...</unclear>

<summary>This page contains a dialogue between Laozi and Shicheng Qi regarding the nature of names, reality, and detachment from worldly labels, accompanied by marginal notes on stylistic and philosophical interpretation.</summary>
<keywords>Laozi, Shicheng Qi, detachment, names and reality, virtue, philosophical commentary</keywords>
